item: Microsoft Post Incident Report, Report Date 20 November 2026
source_access: Microsoft-authored 15-page PDF, opened and text-extracted with pdftotext on 2026-11-24. The copy is hosted by a third party (365Fanatic), not by Microsoft. Full text not committed (Microsoft no-reproduction notice).
defect: Lock contention inside an internal Windows process exhausted CPU and memory on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers used by Exchange Online. 'neither the underlying defect nor the update applies to broader Windows deployments.'
exposure_period: 'The change that introduced the defect started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks... For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact.' The words 'four months' do not appear.
why_testing_missed_it: 'Our normal load testing did not detect the issue because the traffic conditions were different from what was observed during the incident and SKUs used in our labs reduced the likelihood of encountering this defect.' Newer SKUs have more cores and more concurrent requests, so more contention; the load tests used older, fewer-core hardware.
four_factors: (1) connection-processing defect; (2) nearly 14% of gateway server capacity out of service as routine deployment maintenance, with 'enough spare capacity that this reduction in capacity alone would not have caused impact'; (3) Teams failover, at 1:07 AM UTC on 12 November after a routing issue in US East, onto the redundant gateway that also serves Exchange Online; (4) peak load, broad failures from about 4:00 PM UTC as US traffic approached its daily peak. After the Teams shift 'all services continued to remain healthy for the next ~16 hours.'
scope_of_80_percent: 'In less than two hours, this previously unknown defect was triggered across a significant portion of the North American server fleet. At the lowest point, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.' North America, not global.
cascade_mechanism: Traffic management routes around unhealthy 'capacity units' (shards of compute and networking) within a region; remaining units absorbed more load and hit the same defect. When a region ran low, traffic was redirected to other regions that had the same regression. 'Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally.'
why_recovery_took_longer: Servers returning to service 'were immediately overwhelmed by queuing client traffic and became unresponsive again. Our automated recovery processes were not equipped to restore service reliably under this combination...' The defect came from a change months earlier, so change auditing and diagnostics were slow to identify it.
no_rollback: 'our usual safeguards for recent changes (stopping a config rollout, rolling back a deployment, or switching off a newly enabled feature) could not quickly revert it.' The defect was already in the worldwide fleet, so recovery ran per capacity unit across the globe.
five_step_fix: Take the server out of service; restart it from its unresponsive state; apply the patch; restart again; return it to service.
timeline_utc: Incident start 12 Nov 4:20 PM UTC. 7:00 PM all deployments and config changes paused. 8:00 PM bypass of failing health checks. 9:00 PM alternative health check. 11:55 PM returned servers became unresponsive again on receiving traffic. 13 Nov 7:20 AM update reverting the defective change applied to part of the capacity. 11:00 AM Asia Pacific, 11:35 AM Europe, 2:17 PM global webmail, 3:54 PM most major access methods recovered. 4:10 PM no longer active impact. 14 Nov 4:15 AM declared resolved.
duration_variants: From 4:20 PM UTC 12 Nov to 4:10 PM UTC 13 Nov is 23 hours 50 minutes of impact. LeadDev says 'Twenty hours' and 'the better part of a day'. Check against the report before using any single figure.
customer_notification_delay: 'First customer notification came about 20 minutes after broad impact.' On-call was alerted 4:20 PM UTC; first Service Health Dashboard post EX1550543 at 4:20 PM; MO1550821 at 6:27 PM.
corrective_actions: Completed: reverted update; Windows image permanently updated; mail retry window extended from 24 to 48 hours; capacity added; monitoring added; temporary guardrails against automatic traffic distribution. Next steps (13 rows, dates CY26 Q4 to CY27 Q1 or TBD) include fixing cross-region cascade, partitioning gateway capacity by workload, regional-only Teams failover, failover testing at peak conditions, gradual ramp-up and admission control when servers rejoin, retry and back-off, and 'expanding load testing to our newest, highest-core hardware and with production-representative traffic, including running regular tests at peak-load limits.' (CY27Q1)
other_statements: 'This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity. This change was not caused by AI tooling.' 'No mail was lost' for enterprise messages; some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days expired and senders got non-delivery reports.
